nameStory: The name 'hazel' comes from the Old English 'haesel,' which traces back to ancient Germanic words meaning 'twig' or 'rod.' This perfectly captures how people have used hazel's flexible branches for centuries - from basket weaving to building fences. The word 'avellana' in its scientific name honors the Italian town of Avella, famous for producing excellent hazelnuts in Roman times.
description: Common hazel is a multi-stemmed shrub that grows 10-26 feet tall, creating dense thickets of arching branches. Originally from Europe and western Asia, it's occasionally found in New England as an escaped cultivated plant. This is the shrub that produces the round hazelnuts (or cob nuts) you might buy at the grocery store. Its flexible branches and heart-shaped leaves make it look quite different from our native hazelnuts.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round hazelnuts enclosed in leafy, frilly husks that split open when ripe - distinctly rounder than our native hazelnuts which are more egg-shaped

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with doubly-serrated edges that feel soft and slightly fuzzy on the underside, arranged alternately on branches

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multi-stemmed shrub forming dense clumps with smooth, flexible branches that bend easily without breaking

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Male flowers hang in long, dangling yellow catkins in early spring before leaves emerge, while tiny red female flowers appear as small buds on the same plant

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, gray-brown bark on younger stems that may develop shallow furrows on older, thicker trunks

habitat: Rare in New England, occasionally found near old homesteads, abandoned farms, or naturalized from cultivation in disturbed areas. Prefers well-drained soils in partially sunny locations. Most likely encountered in southern New England where it may persist from historical plantings or escape from modern cultivation.

seasonality.spring: Yellow male catkins dangle prominently before leaves emerge, making this the best time for identification. Tiny red female flowers appear as small tufts on branch tips.
seasonality.summer: Heart-shaped leaves are fully developed and nuts begin forming inside their distinctive frilly green husks.
seasonality.fall: Nuts ripen and husks turn brown and papery, splitting to reveal round hazelnuts. Leaves turn yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show next year's catkins as small, hard clusters, and the multi-stemmed growth pattern is clearly visible.

funFact: Hazel branches were traditionally used as 'divining rods' to locate underground water sources - a practice called dowsing that's still done today, though science can't explain why some people swear it works!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with native American hazelnut, but common hazel has rounder nuts and tends to grow taller with a more upright habit. The nuts are the giveaway - common hazel nuts are distinctly round like marbles, while native hazelnut produces more elongated, egg-shaped nuts.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'common' hazel, it's actually quite uncommon in New England since it's not native here. The hazelnuts sold commercially are usually from this European species, not our native American hazelnuts. Don't confuse the edible hazelnuts with witch hazel, which is a completely different plant family despite the similar name.
compareHints: Common hazel differs from our native hazelnuts by producing round nuts instead of elongated ones, and growing taller with a more upright habit. American hazelnut rarely exceeds 10 feet and spreads by underground runners, while beaked hazelnut has distinctive long, beaked husks that extend well beyond the nut. Common hazel's husks are frilly but don't extend into long tubes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's hazelnuts, beaked hazelnut is distinguished by its dramatically extended nut husks that form a long tube or 'beak.
American hazelnut differs from its cousin beaked hazelnut mainly in the nut husks - American's are shorter and more open, while beaked hazelnut's extend into a long, narrow tube beyond the nut.
Turkish hazel towers over its New England relatives - our native American and beaked hazelnuts are shrubs that rarely exceed 15 feet, while Turkish hazel can reach 80 feet.
